newsitem.title: USA: U.S. studies ways to bring Pol Pot to trial.
newsitem.headline: U.S. studies ways to bring Pol Pot to trial.

text.p: The United States is studying different ways of bringing Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot to trial on genocide charges, assuming he can be taken into custody, the State Department said on Tuesday.

"We're looking at any option that may be available to help the Cambodian people," said John Dinger, a department spokesman. "We're investigating a wide range of options. We will follow the Cambodians' lead."

The United States apparently has no laws on its books that would provide jurisdiction over Pol Pot if he were handed over by the Khmer Rouge faction that says it is holding him at Anlong Veng, a guerrilla redoubt near the Thai border.

The Justice Department has been looking into whether Washington has "criminal jurisdiction over anything that Pol Pot did" during his brutal, ultra-revolutionary rule from 1975 through 1978, the State Department's top lawyer, Michael Matheson, said in an interview.
But so far, Justice Department lawyers have found no statutes that could be applied, a department spokesman, John Russell, said.

The extraterritorial reach of U.S. anti-terrorism laws was enacted largely in the 1980s, after the death of more than one million Cambodians under Khmer Rouge rule. U.S. law cannot be applied retroactively, even though at least four U.S. citizens apparently were executed by the Khmer Rouge.

One possibility under review by U.S. officials is the creation by treaty of an international tribunal that could try Pol Pot for genocide as defined by the Genocide Convention adopted by the United Nations in 1948.
Diplomats in New York said such a panel could be set up by expanding the existing U.N. war crimes tribunals on the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda.

Setting up a tribunal by treaty would preclude any veto by China, a Security Council member that may be cool to an airing of information about its own dealings with Pol Pot, a onetime ally against Vietnam.

On Saturday, both of Cambodia's two prime ministers signed a request to the United Nations for help in setting up a tribunal outside the country to try Pol Pot for crimes against humanity. They fear any trial inside Cambodia could stir new violent clashes.

"By asking the international community to help it bring Pol Pot to justice, the Cambodian government has opened up a broad range of possibilities," said Diane Orentlicher, a professor of international law at American University.
Orentlicher, director of the law school's war crimes research office, said one possible forum would be a collective project of willing states, undertaken with U.N. blessings.
Such a solution would avoid the bureaucracy of the United Nations, satisfying one of the concerns of the United States, which has asked Canada to let Pol Pot be transferred there for a trial.
Canada has a law on its books that explicitly covers crimes against humanity -- essentially atrocities on a mass scale against civilians -- as well as war crimes.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Tuesday at the United Nations that Canada had made no decision on the U.S. request but "if we can do something we will."

According to an expert on Cambodia who has documented the Khmer Rouge reign of terror and who asked not to be named, four Americans were killed in 1978 at Tuol Sleng, a school near Phnom Penh that was turned into a torture centre where about 20,000 people died.

He identified the U.S. victims as James Clark, Lance McNamara, Michael Deeds and Christopher Lance. Hometowns were not immediately available. They were seized in two separate incidents from pleasure craft in waters off Cambodia in the Gulf of Thailand and killed as CIA spies, the scholar said.
